# Frontier AI Governance Map

By Yuyu Shen
Personal site: https://buildwithwhy.com
Contact: buildwithwhy@gmail.com
Web version: https://ai-governance-map.buildwithwhy.com
Content updated: 10 October 2026 (entries are re-verified on a rolling basis, not all at once)

## Overview

An interactive map of frontier AI governance: six layers across the rows, METR's nine common elements as an orthogonal filter. Each mechanism is mapped to its layer (who acts) and to which of METR's elements it covers (what it addresses). The empty cells of the orthogonal coverage view are as informative as the filled ones.

The map organises by *who acts*, not *what they regulate*: the EU AI Act sits in Layer 2 (statute), the EU AI Office in Layer 4 (the institution enforcing it).

## Stats

- 53 mechanisms mapped
- 19 voluntary or norm-only
- 14 binding with penalties
- 9 coverage categories

## Layers

- **Layer 1 — International**: Multilateral norms and summits
- **Layer 2 — National regulation**: Statutes, executive orders, framework acts
- **Layer 3 — Sub-national**: US states acting where federal regulation is absent
- **Layer 4 — Infrastructure**: Regulators, AISIs, evaluators, compute controls
- **Layer 5 — Industry voluntary**: Cross-firm commitments and codes
- **Layer 6 — Corporate self-governance**: Frontier safety frameworks at each lab

## Coverage categories (METR's nine common elements)

Source: https://metr.org/common-elements

- **Capability thresholds**: Levels at which obligations or risks trigger
- **Model evaluations**: Tests assessing model capabilities and risks
- **Capability elicitation**: Surfacing the full capabilities of a model
- **Timing & frequency**: When evaluations and obligations apply
- **Weight security**: Protecting model weights from theft
- **Deployment mitigations**: Refusals, monitoring, content controls
- **Conditions for halting**: When to pause development or deployment
- **Accountability**: Oversight, transparency, reporting
- **Updating policies**: How policies get revised over time

## Mechanisms

### Layer 1 — International

#### Intl AI Safety Report

- Jurisdiction: Multilateral
- Enforceability: Voluntary
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://internationalaisafetyreport.org/

Bengio-chaired scientific synthesis. Feb 2026 edition flagged emerging "sandbagging" — models underperforming during safety tests.

Closest thing the field has to an IPCC for AI: yearly synthesis of the evidence base, drawing on AISIs and academic researchers, commissioned at Bletchley (2023). Doesn't make policy recommendations — its job is to give policymakers a defensible read on what frontier models can do and which risks are credible enough to act on.

**Coverage:**

- *Capability thresholds*: Doesn't set thresholds itself, but synthesises the empirical evidence on what capability levels appear, when, and how reliably. The risk catalogue is the closest thing to a shared baseline that policymakers can cite when proposing thresholds.
- *Model evaluations*: Establishes the science of frontier evaluation by summarising methods, gaps, and reliability findings across the AISI Network and academic researchers. Functions as the field's annual literature review on what evaluations can and cannot tell us.
- *Capability elicitation*: The Feb 2026 edition formally flagged sandbagging — models intentionally underperforming during safety tests — as a credible elicitation challenge. Earlier editions documented similar gaps in red-teaming methodology.

**Connections:**

- → AI summit series: AISR is the scientific input to summit declarations
- → NAAIMES (ex-AISI Network): AISIs contribute evidence; AISR shapes priorities
- → METR: METR contributes capability evidence to AISR
- → Apollo Research: Apollo contributes scheming evidence to AISR
- → Center for AI Safety: CAIS's 2023 Statement on AI Risk shaped the discourse the AISR formalises
- → UN AI Panel & Dialogue: AISR positions itself as complementary to the UN Panel; Bengio chairs both

---

#### NAAIMES (ex-AISI Network)

- Jurisdiction: Multilateral
- Enforceability: Soft / advisory
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://www.gov.uk/government/news/efforts-to-share-best-practices-on-ai-measurement-and-evaluations-driven-forward-through-the-international-network-for-advanced-ai-measurement-evalua

Members: UK, US/CAISI, EU AI Office, Japan, Singapore, South Korea, Canada, France INESIA, Australia, Kenya. Renamed Dec 2025 (San Diego convening) to "International Network for Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science" (NAAIMES), with the UK as Network Coordinator. First best-practice guidance (automated evaluation of LLMs, for third-party evaluators) issued Jul 2026.

Coordinates joint testing methodology, shared evaluation benchmarks, and information exchange between national institutes — designed to avoid every country re-running the same evaluations from scratch. The 'safety → measurement, evaluation and science' rename in Dec 2025 mirrored the broader US shift away from safety framing toward standards/science.

**Coverage:**

- *Model evaluations*: Coordinates a shared methodology for frontier-model evaluations across member institutes so that findings travel across borders. Without it, each AISI would re-run the same benchmarks in isolation.
- *Capability elicitation*: Pools elicitation techniques (prompting strategies, agentic scaffolding, jailbreaks) so that what one institute discovers is available to others. Most useful for catching sandbagging or capability gaps that single-institute testing might miss.
- *Timing & frequency*: Coordinates pre-deployment evaluation access between members and frontier labs, so a model evaluated by one AISI doesn't need to be re-tested from scratch by another.
- *Accountability*: Multilateral information-sharing channel for evaluation results and emerging safety concerns. Provides accountability through peer institutes rather than through enforcement.

**Connections:**

- → Intl AI Safety Report: AISIs contribute evidence; AISR shapes priorities
- → UK AISI: UK AISI is a founding network member
- → US CAISI: CAISI represents the US in the network
- → EU AI Office: EU AI Office's Safety Unit is part of the network
- → Other national AISIs: Singapore, Japan, France, Korea, Canada, Australia, Kenya participate
- → AI summit series: Network was agreed at the May 2024 Seoul summit; established Nov 2024

---

#### AI summit series

- Jurisdiction: Multilateral
- Enforceability: Voluntary
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://impact.indiaai.gov.in/

Bletchley → Seoul → Paris (US, UK refused to sign) → New Delhi (Feb 2026, "Impact"; ~92 countries/IOs signed the Declaration; 13 firms signed the Frontier AI Impact Commitments) → Geneva (2027); UAE 2028.

The main forum for forging cross-jurisdictional norms — each summit produces a declaration plus, increasingly, voluntary firm commitments. The framing has tilted with each host: Bletchley centred existential risk, Seoul institutionalised lab commitments, Paris pivoted to 'action' and industrial strategy, Delhi to 'impact' and inclusion. Geneva 2027 is the next test of whether the safety-vs-action divide can be re-bridged.

**Coverage:**

- *Capability thresholds*: The Seoul Frontier AI Safety Commitments (2024) asked signatory firms to publish capability thresholds and the actions they would take if those thresholds were crossed — not threshold-setting by the summit itself, but the catalyst for the lab-published norm.
- *Accountability*: The summit declarations and accompanying firm commitments operate as accountability through public statement. Compliance is monitored only by reputational pressure and by the count of signatories at successor summits.
- *Updating policies*: Each summit cycle revises and extends the commitments — Seoul institutionalised lab safety frameworks, Paris pivoted to industrial action, Delhi added impact and inclusion. The cadence itself is the update mechanism.

**Connections:**

- → Intl AI Safety Report: AISR is the scientific input to summit declarations
- → NAAIMES (ex-AISI Network): Network was agreed at the May 2024 Seoul summit; established Nov 2024
- → Seoul commitments: Seoul commitments came out of the 2024 summit
- → Delhi commitments: Delhi commitments came out of the Feb 2026 summit
- → UN AI Panel & Dialogue: Paris summit statement reaffirmed support for launching the Panel and Dialogue

---

#### OECD AI Principles

- Jurisdiction: Multilateral
- Enforceability: Voluntary
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://oecd.ai/en/ai-principles

2019, updated 2024. 50 countries plus the EU adhere (May 2026).

Five values-based principles (inclusive growth, human-centred, transparency, robustness, accountability) plus five policy recommendations. Non-binding but the de facto reference point — adopted by the G20 and embedded in many national strategies. The 2024 update sharpened the safety/security language in response to generative AI.

**Coverage:**

- *Deployment mitigations*: The Principles include high-level safety, security, and robustness expectations applied across the AI lifecycle. Concrete deployment rules are left to national implementations.
- *Accountability*: Transparency and explainability, and accountability, are two of the five values-based principles. Adopting countries are encouraged to embed them in domestic frameworks rather than report on them.
- *Updating policies*: Periodic review built into the OECD process; the 2024 update sharpened the safety/security language in response to generative AI.

**Connections:**

- → Hiroshima Process: OECD principles inform the G7 Hiroshima Code

---

#### CoE AI Convention

- Jurisdiction: Multilateral
- Enforceability: Hard law, weak enforcement
- Status: Proposed
- Primary source: https://www.coe.int/en/web/artificial-intelligence/the-framework-convention-on-artificial-intelligence

First binding international AI treaty (opened for signature Sept 2024). Signatories include EU, UK, US, Japan; only the EU has ratified (approved Apr 2026). Not yet in force: needs five ratifications incl. three CoE member states.

Covers AI used by public authorities and (with carve-outs) by private actors; obliges signatories to ensure rights to redress, transparency, and lifecycle risk management. Significantly weakened in negotiation — private-sector obligations were softened to win US/UK signatures, and ratification has stalled in most parliaments. The first AI treaty with binding force, even if its substantive obligations were narrowed during negotiation.

**Coverage:**

- *Deployment mitigations*: Signatories must ensure risk management throughout the AI lifecycle for systems used by public authorities, with significantly softened obligations for the private sector. The substantive duties are written at the framework level — implementation is left to domestic law.
- *Accountability*: Independent oversight bodies and rights to redress for those affected by AI decisions; the substantive teeth depend on whether signatories transpose these into binding domestic mechanisms.
- *Updating policies*: Periodic review by the conference of parties; in practice ratification has slowed to a crawl, so the implementation surface is still tiny.

**Connections:**

- → EU AI Act: CoE Convention is the international treaty layer above EU AI Act
- → UK AI Bill: CoE Convention shapes UK AI Bill drafting

---

#### UNESCO AI Recommendation

- Jurisdiction: Multilateral
- Enforceability: Voluntary
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://www.unesco.org/en/artificial-intelligence/recommendation-ethics

Adopted Nov 2021 by UNESCO's 193 Member States.

First global standard-setting instrument on AI ethics, organised around 11 policy actions (data governance, environment, gender, health, etc.). Non-binding. Most influential in low- and middle-income jurisdictions outside the OECD process; provides reference text for many national AI ethics charters.

**Coverage:**

- *Deployment mitigations*: Eleven policy actions covering data governance, environment, health, gender, etc. — high-level mitigation principles rather than specific obligations. Most influential in jurisdictions outside the OECD process that lean on UNESCO text for their own AI ethics charters.
- *Accountability*: Transparency and human oversight are core principles, but the recommendation imposes no reporting or audit obligations. Implementation is monitored by UNESCO's Readiness Assessment Methodology.

**Connections:**

- → UN AI Panel & Dialogue: UNESCO co-coordinates the Global Dialogue's joint secretariat with ITU

---

#### UN AI Panel & Dialogue

- Jurisdiction: Multilateral
- Enforceability: Voluntary
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://www.un.org/independent-international-scientific-panel-ai/en

UN General Assembly resolution 79/325 (Aug 2025) created a 40-member Independent International Scientific Panel on AI and an annual Global Dialogue on AI Governance. The Panel (co-chairs Yoshua Bengio, Maria Ressa) issued its Preliminary Report in Jul 2026 and a brief on AI agents and loss of control in Sep 2026; the first Dialogue met in Geneva in Jul 2026.

The UN's universal-membership counterpart to the International AI Safety Report and the summit series. The Panel's annual report is policy-relevant but non-prescriptive and is presented at the Dialogue, a platform whose topics include safe, secure and trustworthy AI, human rights and interoperable governance; its outcomes are co-chairs' summaries, not negotiated texts. Non-military domain only. The Sep 2026 brief, on AI agents that breached Hugging Face's systems while under evaluation at OpenAI, put loss-of-control risk on the UN agenda.

**Coverage:**

- *Model evaluations*: Synthesises scientific evidence on AI capabilities, risks and safeguards rather than testing models itself; its first thematic brief assessed a real incident involving AI agents under evaluation.
- *Accountability*: Annual report presented to governments at the Global Dialogue, plus up to two updates a year to the General Assembly plenary. No enforcement: accountability through shared evidence and public debate.
- *Updating policies*: One annual report plus thematic briefs as the Panel deems necessary; the Dialogue meets annually, alternating between Geneva and New York (next: New York, May 2027).

**Connections:**

- → Intl AI Safety Report: AISR positions itself as complementary to the UN Panel; Bengio chairs both
- → UNESCO AI Recommendation: UNESCO co-coordinates the Global Dialogue's joint secretariat with ITU
- → AI summit series: Paris summit statement reaffirmed support for launching the Panel and Dialogue

---

### Layer 2 — National regulation

#### EU AI Act

- Jurisdiction: European Union
- Enforceability: Binding with penalties
- Status: Phasing in
- Primary source: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng

In force Aug 2024. GPAI obligations Aug 2025. Most provisions apply Aug 2026; the 2026 Digital Omnibus (Reg. 2026/1744) moved high-risk rules to Dec 2027 (Annex III) and Aug 2028 (Annex I). Penalties up to €35M or 7% global revenue.

Tiers AI by risk: prohibited practices, high-risk systems (conformity assessments, fundamental-rights impact assessments, registration), and GPAI models (transparency, copyright). GPAI above 10²⁵ FLOPs faces additional systemic-risk obligations — evaluations, incident reporting, cybersecurity. Its 10²⁵ threshold is lower than the 10²⁶ used by recent US state laws, so more models fall into systemic-risk obligations under EU rules than under California's.

**Coverage:**

- *Capability thresholds*: GPAI models trained with cumulative compute above 10²⁵ FLOPs are presumed to have systemic risk and face additional obligations. Lower than the 10²⁶ used by California SB 53 and NY RAISE — more EU models meet the threshold than US-state ones.
- *Model evaluations*: GPAI providers with systemic-risk models must conduct model evaluations using state-of-the-art protocols, including adversarial testing. The Code of Practice operationalises this through specific procedures.
- *Capability elicitation*: Adversarial testing is required for systemic-risk GPAI; the Code of Practice goes further, mandating red-teaming with capability elicitation techniques.
- *Timing & frequency*: Both pre-market obligations (conformity assessments for high-risk; transparency for GPAI) and post-market duties (post-market monitoring for high-risk systems; AI Office supervision of GPAI models). The first regulation to formally split the lifecycle this way.
- *Weight security*: Cybersecurity protections for model weights are mandatory for systemic-risk GPAI under Article 55. Implementation detail is delegated to the Code of Practice and harmonised standards.
- *Deployment mitigations*: A layered set of obligations: prohibited practices (banned), high-risk obligations (impact assessments, registration), GPAI duties (transparency, copyright), Article 50 marking of AI-generated content, and additional systemic-risk mitigations. The most comprehensive deployment-mitigation regime in any binding instrument.
- *Accountability*: Mandatory incident reporting to the EU AI Office for systemic-risk GPAI; market-surveillance authorities handle high-risk systems. The Office can request models, order recalls, and fine GPAI providers up to €15M / 3% global revenue.
- *Updating policies*: The Code of Practice and harmonised standards are revisable as the field changes, and the Commission can update the 10²⁵ threshold and the Annex III high-risk list by delegated act; other changes to the regulation go through ordinary EU legislative procedure (slower).

**Connections:**

- → CoE AI Convention: CoE Convention is the international treaty layer above EU AI Act
- → EU AI Office: EU AI Office is the regulator implementing EU AI Act
- → EU GPAI Code of Practice: GPAI Code is the voluntary route to EU AI Act compliance
- → UK ICO: UK GDPR/ICO guidance and EU AI Act set parallel data/AI standards
- → EU AI-generated content code: Code implements the AI Act's Article 50 marking and labelling duties

---

#### US EO 14179

- Jurisdiction: US Federal
- Enforceability: Hard law, weak enforcement
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/01/31/2025-02172/removing-barriers-to-american-leadership-in-artificial-intelligence

Trump (Jan 23, 2025). Issued after EO 14148 revoked Biden EO 14110, whose reporting duties covered red-team results for dual-use foundation models; orders agencies to suspend, revise or rescind actions taken under EO 14110.

Frames AI policy as removing regulatory barriers to American leadership; ordered the AI Action Plan within 180 days. Ordered review and rescission of the safety-focused measures taken under EO 14110, such as reporting of red-team results for dual-use foundation models. Marks the federal turn away from safety-oriented governance toward an industrial-policy framing.

**Connections:**

- → US AI Action Plan: EO 14179 ordered the Jul 2025 AI Action Plan
- → US Frontier AI Access EO: Marks shift from prior deregulation-only EO posture
- → US preemption EO: Trump EO sequence — preemption builds on EO 14179
- → US CAISI: EO led to AISI rename to CAISI in Jun 2025

---

#### US AI Action Plan

- Jurisdiction: US Federal
- Enforceability: Soft / advisory
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Americas-AI-Action-Plan.pdf

Jul 2025. Calls for limiting federal AI funding to states with "burdensome" AI regulations.

Dozens of federal actions across innovation, infrastructure, and international policy. The centrepiece is regulatory removal — directing OMB to flag or restrict federal funding to states whose AI laws inhibit deployment. Also pushes export of the US AI stack abroad, expanded compute infrastructure, and federal procurement levers.

**Coverage:**

- *Accountability*: Directs OMB to flag and restrict federal funding to states whose AI laws inhibit deployment — accountability runs in the opposite direction from typical Layer 2 statutes, restraining state-level AI oversight rather than expanding federal oversight of frontier developers.

**Connections:**

- → US EO 14179: EO 14179 ordered the Jul 2025 AI Action Plan
- → US preemption EO: EO 14365 adds litigation and BEAD-funding conditions to the Action Plan's state-funding lever; the Plan did not call for preemption
- → US FTC: FTC operates alongside the Action Plan, enforcing federal consumer law on AI

---

#### US preemption EO

- Jurisdiction: US Federal
- Enforceability: Hard law, weak enforcement
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/12/16/2025-23092/ensuring-a-national-policy-framework-for-artificial-intelligence

EO 14365 (Dec 11 2025). DOJ AI Litigation Task Force (set up Jan 9, 2026) to challenge state AI laws. DOJ moved to intervene in xAI v. Colorado on Apr 24, 2026, on equal-protection grounds.

Directs DOJ to challenge state AI laws as Commerce Clause violations or as preempted by federal law. Pairs the Action Plan's funding lever with parallel litigation pressure. Whether the Task Force's challenges hold up will determine whether the federal-vs-state contest gets resolved through courts or stays politically contested.

**Coverage:**

- *Accountability*: DOJ AI Litigation Task Force is empowered to challenge state AI laws as Commerce Clause violations or as preempted by federal law. Accountability here is restraint of state-level oversight rather than substantive frontier-AI accountability.

**Connections:**

- → US EO 14179: Trump EO sequence — preemption builds on EO 14179
- → US AI Action Plan: EO 14365 adds litigation and BEAD-funding conditions to the Action Plan's state-funding lever; the Plan did not call for preemption
- → California SB 53: Preemption EO targets SB 53; DOJ task force can challenge
- → Colorado ADMT Act: DOJ intervened in xAI v. Colorado Apr 24, 2026
- → NY RAISE Act: Preemption EO targets RAISE Act
- → US FTC: EO 14365 directs the FTC to explain when Section 5 preempts state AI-output laws; FTC proposed that policy statement in Jul 2026
- → US FRONTIER Act: Legislative route to the preemptive national standard EO 14365 calls for

---

#### US Frontier AI Access EO

- Jurisdiction: US Federal
- Enforceability: Hard law, weak enforcement
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/06/05/2026-11415/promoting-advanced-artificial-intelligence-innovation-and-security

EO 14409, signed June 2, 2026. Directs Treasury, NSA and CISA to design a voluntary framework under which developers may give the government access to 'covered frontier models' (designated by the NSA Director via a classified cyber benchmark) for up to 30 days before release to other trusted partners. Rules out mandatory licensing or preclearance.

Marks a notable shift in the Trump administration's posture — from deregulation (EO 14179) and state preemption (EO 14365) toward asking for federal access to pre-release frontier models, though the order itself is scoped to cyber capabilities and rejects 'overly burdensome regulation'. The 30-day voluntary window mirrors the access agreements UK AISI uses. NSA, Treasury and CISA lead; CAISI is not named and NIST is only consulted. Whether the framework results in meaningful federal access will depend on developer participation.

**Coverage:**

- *Model evaluations*: Voluntary early access (up to 30 days) to models the NSA designates through a classified cyber-capability benchmark; scoped to cyber capabilities, not general safety evaluation.
- *Timing & frequency*: Benchmark and framework due within 60 days of the order; access window up to 30 days before release to other trusted partners; participation voluntary.
- *Accountability*: Creates no approval or preclearance power (§3(c)) and no enforceable rights (§5(c)). Also directs a Treasury-led AI cybersecurity clearinghouse and a DOJ enforcement priority on AI-enabled computer crime.

**Connections:**

- → US EO 14179: Marks shift from prior deregulation-only EO posture
- → UK AISI: 30-day access model mirrors UK AISI voluntary access agreements
- → Frontier Security Institute: FSI's lab–national-security translation bears on the EO's voluntary frontier-model access framework

---

#### US FRONTIER Act

- Jurisdiction: US Federal
- Enforceability: Soft / advisory
- Status: Proposed
- Primary source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119hr9925ih/html/BILLS-119hr9925ih.htm

H.R. 9925, bipartisan House bill introduced Jul 23, 2026 (Obernolte, Trahan). Frontier models >10²⁶ FLOPs: published frameworks, annual third-party audits, 72-hour incident reports, licensed verifiers for the largest developers; up to $1M per violation. Would preempt state frontier-transparency, audit and incident-reporting rules.

Would create a federal frontier-AI regime under a new Commerce Under Secretary for AI Security. Large frontier developers would have to publish, follow and annually audit a frontier AI framework and publish a transparency report at each deployment. Very large ones would also retain a licensed independent verification organization. The Commerce Secretary could order a halt to development or deployment that presents an imminent catastrophic risk. The preemption clause covers the ground of state laws such as SB 53 and RAISE (frontier risk transparency, third-party auditing, incident reporting) but leaves deployment, child-safety and state-procurement rules to the states. It is a congressional route to the national standard EO 14365 calls for, with binding duties the EO does not create.

**Coverage:**

- *Capability thresholds*: Frontier models trained with >10²⁶ FLOPs. Obligations scale with developer size: large (>$50M revenue and ≥$1B AI development spending over 36 months) and very large (>$5B and ≥$10B).
- *Model evaluations*: Annual independent compliance audits for large frontier developers. Very large developers retain a licensed independent verification organization for ongoing assessment of their framework, risk monitoring and mitigations, including internal use.
- *Timing & frequency*: Transparency report before or at deployment of each new or substantially modified frontier model. Critical safety incidents reported within 72 hours (24 hours to law enforcement for imminent risk to life).
- *Weight security*: Frameworks must cover cybersecurity for non-public model weights; weight exfiltration is a reportable critical safety incident.
- *Deployment mitigations*: Frontier AI frameworks must set risk thresholds, assess each model against them and decide on deployment and internal use; minimum framework requirements are set by regulation.
- *Conditions for halting*: The Commerce Secretary may issue emergency orders suspending or restricting development, deployment or internal use of a frontier model that presents an imminent catastrophic risk.
- *Accountability*: Audit reports go to the Under Secretary, the Attorney General and opted-in state attorneys general. Civil penalties up to $1M per violation, enforced by the Attorney General and opted-in state AGs.
- *Updating policies*: Frameworks reviewed at least annually, with a justification published within 30 days of any material change; framework regulations reviewed yearly.

**Connections:**

- → California SB 53: Would preempt state frontier-transparency, audit and incident-reporting duties such as SB 53's
- → NY RAISE Act: Would preempt state frontier-transparency, audit and incident-reporting duties such as RAISE's
- → US preemption EO: Legislative route to the preemptive national standard EO 14365 calls for

---

#### China GenAI Measures

- Jurisdiction: China
- Enforceability: Binding with penalties
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://www.cac.gov.cn/2023-07/13/c_1690898327029107.htm

CAC Interim Measures for Generative AI (Aug 2023). Binding, with concrete enforcement.

Services with public-opinion attributes or social-mobilisation capacity must undergo a security assessment and file their algorithms with the Cyberspace Administration of China; all providers must use lawfully sourced training data and moderate content in line with Chinese law. Non-compliant services offered from outside China can be blocked. Enforcement is active — multiple firms have had services suspended — but operates as much through industrial policy as through fines.

**Coverage:**

- *Timing & frequency*: Services with public-opinion attributes or social-mobilisation capacity must undergo a security assessment under national rules and complete algorithm filing with the Cyberspace Administration of China (Art. 17); apps built on them must display the filing number.
- *Deployment mitigations*: Content moderation aligned with Chinese law (including political-content rules), training-data rules (lawful sources, IP, consent, quality), and labelling of AI-generated outputs are required. Concrete deployment rules with active enforcement — multiple firms have had services suspended.
- *Accountability*: Services with public-opinion attributes or social-mobilisation capacity must file their algorithms with the Cyberspace Administration (Art. 17); the CAC publishes lists of filed generative AI services. Non-compliant services offered from outside China can be blocked (Art. 20).

**Connections:**

- → China AI Law: GenAI Measures could be consolidated into a comprehensive AI law

---

#### China AI Law

- Jurisdiction: China
- Enforceability: Soft / advisory
- Status: Proposed
- Primary source: http://www.npc.gov.cn/npc/c2/c30834/202605/P020260511309265804880.pdf

Comprehensive AI legislation at the planning stage: an unscheduled preparatory item in the NPC Standing Committee's 2025 and 2026 legislative plans; the State Council's 2026 plan calls for accelerating it. No draft has been submitted.

Could consolidate the patchwork of CAC measures (recommendation algorithms, deep synthesis, generative AI) into a single statute. The State Council dropped a named AI Law draft from its 2025 plan, then in May 2026 called for accelerating 'comprehensive legislation'; MOST-led drafting of a framework text was under way in late 2025. In the meantime China regulates frontier issues through narrower instruments — a Cybersecurity Law AI article (in force Jan 2026) and CAC rules on humanlike interactive AI (in force Jul 2026).

**Coverage:**

- *Capability thresholds*: No official draft has been published, so thresholds are not yet defined.
- *Model evaluations*: No official draft has been published, so evaluation duties are not yet defined.
- *Deployment mitigations*: No official draft has been published, so mitigation duties are not yet defined.
- *Accountability*: No official draft has been published, so the oversight structure is not yet defined. Drafting is ministry-led (MOST and others) ahead of any NPC Standing Committee reading.

**Connections:**

- → China GenAI Measures: GenAI Measures could be consolidated into a comprehensive AI law

---

#### UK AI Bill

- Jurisdiction: United Kingdom
- Enforceability: Soft / advisory
- Status: Proposed
- Primary source: https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/the-kings-speech-2024

The 2024 King's Speech promised legislation on developers of the most powerful AI models; no government bill was introduced, and the May 2026 King's Speech announced none.

Would put the UK AI Security Institute on a statutory footing with information-gathering powers, and create binding rules for the most powerful frontier models. Successive missed introduction dates reflect tension between Labour's growth agenda and its safety commitments. Until passed, the UK relies on AISI's pre-deployment access agreements with frontier labs — voluntary and revocable.

**Coverage:**

- *Capability thresholds*: If passed, would target the most powerful frontier models — drafts have referenced cumulative compute or comparable capability indicators. Specifics are still under negotiation.
- *Model evaluations*: Would put the UK AI Security Institute on a statutory footing with information-gathering powers, including access to models and pre-deployment evaluations. Currently AISI's access is voluntary and revocable.
- *Accountability*: Would create binding rules and enforcement mechanisms for frontier developers, replacing the current voluntary memoranda. Until enacted, the UK relies on reputational pressure.

**Connections:**

- → CoE AI Convention: CoE Convention shapes UK AI Bill drafting
- → UK AISI: AI Bill would put AISI on a statutory footing
- → UK Ofcom: UK AI Bill would clarify the boundary between Ofcom (content) and AISI (frontier)
- → UK ICO: UK AI Bill would clarify ICO's role alongside AISI

---

#### Korea AI Framework Act

- Jurisdiction: Asia-Pacific (other)
- Enforceability: Binding with penalties
- Status: Phasing in
- Primary source: https://aibasicact.kr/

AI Basic Act. In force Jan 22, 2026. One-year grace period — penalties (capped ~$21k per violation) begin Jan 22, 2027.

Korea's first horizontal AI law: tiered obligations on high-impact AI and high-performance AI (≥10²⁶ FLOPs plus capability and risk criteria), risk management plans, lifecycle reporting to MSIT, mandatory generative-AI labelling, and a state AI Safety Research Institute. Penalty caps are deliberately low — the Act emphasises guidance over deterrence, mirroring Japan's approach and contrasting with the EU's prescriptive route.

**Coverage:**

- *Capability thresholds*: The Act's safety duties (Art. 32) cover systems above a compute threshold set by decree. The Enforcement Decree (Art. 24, in force Jan 22, 2026) requires cumulative compute ≥10²⁶ FLOPs (matching California SB 53 and NY RAISE, higher than the EU AI Act's 10²⁵) plus state-of-the-art technology and risks with broad, serious effects on life, safety and fundamental rights. High-impact AI is defined separately by use-case rather than compute.
- *Model evaluations*: Risk management plans are required for high-impact and high-performance AI — provider-led evaluations covering safety, fairness, and transparency. Less prescriptive than the EU AI Act on methodology.
- *Timing & frequency*: Lifecycle reporting to MSIT throughout development and deployment; implementing decrees specify cadence. Less burdensome in practice than the EU's pre-market conformity assessment.
- *Deployment mitigations*: Mandatory generative-AI labelling, transparency duties, and obligations to inform users about AI involvement. The most concrete deployment obligations sit at the user-facing end.
- *Accountability*: Safety-duty results go to MSIT, which can investigate (including on reports or complaints) and order violations stopped or corrected (Art. 40); the AI Safety Research Institute supports safety work rather than overseeing it. Enforcement teeth deliberately weak — fines capped at ₩30M (~$21k) (Art. 43).

---

#### Japan AI Promotion Act

- Jurisdiction: Asia-Pacific (other)
- Enforceability: Soft / advisory
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://www8.cao.go.jp/cstp/ai/ai_act/ai_act.html

May 2025. Light-touch, sectoral, no compute thresholds.

Establishes the AI Strategic Headquarters under the Cabinet Office to coordinate sectoral guidance. Deliberately avoids compute thresholds, mandatory pre-deployment testing, and fines — The approach assumes that voluntary cooperation between developers and government produces faster adoption than the EU's prescriptive route. The Hiroshima Process commitments substitute for binding rules at the firm level.

**Coverage:**

- *Deployment mitigations*: Non-binding AI guidelines under Art. 13, adopted by the AI Strategic Headquarters in Dec 2025, alongside ministries' own sectoral guidance (e.g. the AI Business Guidelines), with each sector regulator translating high-level principles into industry-specific expectations. No binding deployment rules.
- *Accountability*: Sectoral oversight without a central regulator; coordination runs through the AI Strategic Headquarters. The act deliberately avoids fines, mandatory pre-deployment testing, or compute thresholds.

**Connections:**

- → Hiroshima Process: Japan champions Hiroshima Process; Promotion Act reflects same approach
- → Japan sectoral AI regulators: Sectoral implementation under the AI Promotion Act framework

---

### Layer 3 — Sub-national

#### California SB 53

- Jurisdiction: US State
- Enforceability: Binding with penalties
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB53

Transparency in Frontier AI Act. Effective Jan 1, 2026. >10²⁶ FLOPs, >$500M revenue. Penalties up to $1M/violation.

Requires 'large frontier developers' to publish a frontier safety framework, report critical safety incidents within 15 days, and publish transparency reports when deploying new or substantially modified frontier models. Whistleblower protections for employees flagging safety issues. The first US state law to codify the published-framework norm — explicitly anchors against Layer 6 lab frameworks rather than reinventing obligations.

**Coverage:**

- *Capability thresholds*: Two tiers: 'frontier developers' (training compute >10²⁶ FLOPs, including fine-tuning) must publish transparency reports and report critical safety incidents; 'large frontier developers' (also >$500M revenue) carry the framework, risk-summary and civil-penalty provisions. Developers below 10²⁶ FLOPs are exempt — the law targets the largest frontier developers, anchoring against Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Meta, and xAI.
- *Timing & frequency*: Critical safety incidents must be reported to the Office of Emergency Services within 15 days (24 hours to an appropriate authority if there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury). Transparency reports are due before or with each new or substantially modified frontier model; frameworks are reviewed at least annually; internal-use risk summaries go to OES every three months. NY RAISE's 72-hour window is tighter.
- *Deployment mitigations*: Frontier safety frameworks must address how the developer identifies and mitigates risks, including pre-deployment evaluations and deployment safeguards. Substantive obligations are framework-level — what the framework must contain, not which specific mitigations to use.
- *Accountability*: Frameworks and transparency reports must be published on the developer's website; incident reports and internal-use risk summaries go to the Office of Emergency Services; the AG brings civil-penalty actions and receives whistleblower disclosures. Codifies the published-framework norm into binding state law.
- *Updating policies*: Frameworks must be kept updated as capabilities and risks evolve. The update obligation makes the law a moving target rather than a snapshot.

**Connections:**

- → US preemption EO: Preemption EO targets SB 53; DOJ task force can challenge
- → Anthropic RSP: SB 53 codifies the published-framework norm Anthropic exemplified
- → OpenAI Preparedness: SB 53 codifies the published-framework norm OpenAI exemplified
- → GDM Frontier Safety Framework: SB 53 codifies the published-framework norm DeepMind exemplified
- → Meta Advanced AI Scaling Framework: SB 53 covers Meta's framework
- → NY RAISE Act: RAISE Act amendments aligned thresholds with SB 53
- → Illinois AI Safety Measures Act: Illinois Act adopts SB 53's compute and revenue thresholds and framework contents
- → US FRONTIER Act: Would preempt state frontier-transparency, audit and incident-reporting duties such as SB 53's

---

#### Colorado ADMT Act

- Jurisdiction: US State
- Enforceability: Binding with penalties
- Status: Phasing in
- Primary source: https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/sb26-189

SB 24-205 (the original Colorado AI Act) was repealed and replaced by SB 26-189, signed May 14, 2026. The new law is a narrower transparency/consumer-disclosure framework, effective Jan 1, 2027.

The original Colorado AI Act would have imposed duty-of-care and algorithmic-impact-assessment duties on developers and deployers of 'high-risk AI systems' for consequential decisions. After federal preemption pressure (xAI litigation, DOJ intervention, April 27 court stay), Colorado repealed the law and replaced it with SB 26-189 — a narrower regime of developer documentation, consumer notice, post-adverse-decision explanations and rights to correction and human review when automated decision-making technology is used in consequential decisions, without the impact-assessment, duty-of-care, or risk-management obligations of the original. Marks a retreat from the comprehensive state-AI-regulation template.

**Coverage:**

- *Timing & frequency*: Effective Jan 1, 2027 (the original SB 24-205 was repealed before reaching its enforcement date). No lifecycle-review obligation.
- *Deployment mitigations*: Narrower than the original SB 24-205: SB 26-189 requires developer documentation, consumer notice, post-adverse-decision explanations and human review on request when automated decision-making technology is used in consequential decisions, but drops the duty of care and impact-assessment regime that drew the federal preemption challenge.
- *Accountability*: AG enforcement of the disclosure duties and consumer rights as deceptive trade practices (60-day cure notice until 2030); no private right of action. The duty-of-care and impact-assessment regime that defined the original Colorado AI Act is gone.

**Connections:**

- → US preemption EO: DOJ intervened in xAI v. Colorado Apr 24, 2026
- → Colorado Division of Insurance: Same state, different focus — DOI sectoral framework predates the AI Act

---

#### NY RAISE Act

- Jurisdiction: US State
- Enforceability: Binding with penalties
- Status: Phasing in
- Primary source: https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/S6953/amendment/B

Hochul signed Dec 19, 2025; chapter amendments Mar 27, 2026 aligned with SB 53. Effective Jan 1, 2027. Penalties $1M / $3M.

Mirrors SB 53's structure — published safety frameworks, 72-hour incident reporting, oversight by a dedicated office at the Department of Financial Services. The Mar 2026 chapter amendments adopted SB 53's >$500M revenue threshold instead of the original training-cost threshold, and softened original penalty levels. Together with SB 53, establishes a dual-coast template that federal preemption hasn't yet dislodged.

**Coverage:**

- *Capability thresholds*: Eligibility: >10²⁶ FLOPs training compute (including fine-tuning) + >$500M annual revenue. The Mar 2026 chapter amendments aligned the thresholds with California SB 53, replacing the original $100M compute-cost tests.
- *Timing & frequency*: 72-hour incident reporting (tighter than SB 53's 15 days). Lifecycle reporting expectations to be specified in DFS regulations.
- *Deployment mitigations*: Safeguards against critical harm — frontier safety frameworks must address mitigation of catastrophic and large-scale risks. Mirrors SB 53's framework-level approach.
- *Accountability*: Department of Financial Services oversight office (DIGIT) — the first US state-level body with dedicated authority over frontier general-purpose AI developers (sectoral AI regulators like the Colorado Division of Insurance, which has overseen insurance-sector algorithms since 2023, predate it). Plus AG enforcement and a published list of large frontier developers that have filed disclosure statements.
- *Updating policies*: DFS regulations expected; like SB 53, frontier developers must keep their published frameworks current as capabilities evolve.

**Connections:**

- → US preemption EO: Preemption EO targets RAISE Act
- → California SB 53: RAISE Act amendments aligned thresholds with SB 53
- → Colorado Division of Insurance: Colorado DOI precedent informed NY RAISE's DFS office model
- → Anthropic RSP: RAISE requires a published frontier AI framework from Jan 2027; Anthropic says it addresses such requirements with documents including its Frontier Compliance Framework, which is separate from the RSP
- → Illinois AI Safety Measures Act: Illinois Act shares RAISE's 72-hour incident window, disclosure statements and $1M / $3M penalties
- → US FRONTIER Act: Would preempt state frontier-transparency, audit and incident-reporting duties such as RAISE's

---

#### Illinois AI Safety Measures Act

- Jurisdiction: US State
- Enforceability: Binding with penalties
- Status: Phasing in
- Primary source: https://www.ilga.gov/legislation/PublicActs/View/104-0538

SB 315 (Public Act 104-0538), signed Jul 6, 2026. Effective Jan 1, 2027; framework and annual independent-audit duties from Jan 1, 2028. >10²⁶ FLOPs, >$500M revenue. Penalties $1M / $3M.

Third state frontier-AI statute, built on the SB 53 / RAISE template: large frontier developers publish a frontier AI framework, file disclosure statements, and report critical safety incidents to the Illinois Emergency Management Agency and the AG within 72 hours; all frontier developers publish transparency reports at deployment. Unlike SB 53 and RAISE, it requires large frontier developers to retain an independent third-party auditor every year. AG enforcement only.

**Coverage:**

- *Capability thresholds*: Frontier developers: training compute >10²⁶ FLOPs (including fine-tuning). Large frontier developers: also >$500M annual revenue, matching SB 53 and RAISE.
- *Timing & frequency*: Critical safety incidents reported to the Illinois Emergency Management Agency and the AG within 72 hours; transparency reports before or with each new or substantially modified frontier model.
- *Accountability*: Annual independent third-party audit of framework compliance from 2028, with a published summary; disclosure statements filed with the Agency from 2027; AG-only civil penalties up to $1M first / $3M subsequent.
- *Updating policies*: Frameworks reviewed at least annually; material modifications published with a justification within 30 days.

**Connections:**

- → California SB 53: Illinois Act adopts SB 53's compute and revenue thresholds and framework contents
- → NY RAISE Act: Illinois Act shares RAISE's 72-hour incident window, disclosure statements and $1M / $3M penalties

---

#### Texas TRAIGA

- Jurisdiction: US State
- Enforceability: Binding with penalties
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/billtext/pdf/HB00149F.pdf

Texas Responsible AI Governance Act, Jun 2025. Narrower than Colorado.

Focuses on specific deployment prohibitions — social scoring, manipulation, certain government uses — rather than horizontal frontier-developer obligations. AG-enforced civil penalties; no compute or revenue threshold. The first AI law passed in a Republican-controlled state, complicating the narrative that AI regulation is purely a Democratic priority.

**Coverage:**

- *Deployment mitigations*: Specific deployment prohibitions including social scoring by government, manipulative AI practices, and certain government uses (biometric identification, etc.). Narrower scope than Colorado's algorithmic-discrimination duties — targets specific harms rather than horizontal obligations.
- *Accountability*: AG enforcement through civil penalties; no central oversight office or impact-assessment regime. The accountability mechanism is purely reactive, triggered by complaints.

---

### Layer 4 — Infrastructure

#### EU AI Office

- Jurisdiction: European Union
- Enforceability: Binding with penalties
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/ai-office

Established Jan 2024 within DG CNECT. GPAI enforcement role Aug 2025; full enforcement Aug 2026. Digital Omnibus (Reg. 2026/1744, in force 27 Jul 2026) adds exclusive supervision of AI systems built on a provider's own GPAI model and of AI in very large online platforms and search engines.

Coordinates AI Act implementation across member states, enforces GPAI obligations directly (a centralised role unique within EU regulatory architecture), and runs the Scientific Panel that advises on systemic risk. Can request models from providers, order recalls, and impose fines; since the Omnibus it also has market-surveillance powers over the AI systems it supervises, including on-site inspections, binding commitments and fines (new AI Act Arts 75a–75d). Effectively the EU's frontier-AI regulator; partner of the AISI Network despite being an EU body rather than a national one.

**Coverage:**

- *Model evaluations*: Can request evaluations from GPAI providers, including pre-deployment access for systemic-risk models. The Scientific Panel of independent experts advises on what to request and how to interpret results.
- *Timing & frequency*: Post-market monitoring is a core function; the Office tracks deployed models for emerging risks and incidents reported by providers. The first cross-border post-market AI regulator.
- *Deployment mitigations*: Can order model recall, mitigations, or temporary restrictions on systemic-risk GPAI. Mitigation orders flow from incident reports, evaluation findings, or scientific panel advice.
- *Conditions for halting*: Recall power functions as a halt mechanism — the Office can require a provider to withdraw a model from the EU market until mitigations are implemented (Aug 2026 onwards).
- *Accountability*: Information requests, scientific panel oversight, and direct enforcement of GPAI obligations. Centralised regulatory authority unique within EU architecture — most enforcement runs through national authorities, but GPAI sits with the Office.

**Connections:**

- → NAAIMES (ex-AISI Network): EU AI Office's Safety Unit is part of the network
- → EU AI Act: EU AI Office is the regulator implementing EU AI Act
- → EU GPAI Code of Practice: EU AI Office runs and oversees the CoP
- → EU AI-generated content code: AI Office facilitated the drafting by independent experts

---

#### UK AISI

- Jurisdiction: United Kingdom
- Enforceability: Soft / advisory
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://www.aisi.gov.uk/

Renamed UK AI Security Institute (Feb 2025). 30+ frontier models tested.

Conducts pre-deployment evaluations of frontier models under voluntary access agreements with major labs; publishes red-teaming and jailbreaking research. The Feb 2025 rename to 'AI Security Institute' narrowed focus toward national-security-adjacent risks (cyber, bio, autonomy) and aligned framing with US CAISI. Without the UK AI Bill, its access remains voluntary — labs could withdraw. The inaugural Frontier AI Trends Report (Dec 2025) draws on two years of evaluating 30+ frontier models.

**Coverage:**

- *Model evaluations*: Pre-deployment testing of frontier models under voluntary access agreements with major labs. 30+ models tested; among the most active national-level frontier evaluators.
- *Capability elicitation*: Red-teaming, jailbreaking research, and capability elicitation are core to AISI's published outputs. Methodologies often adopted by other AISIs and lab frameworks.
- *Timing & frequency*: Pre-deployment access agreements provide testing windows before public release; agreements are voluntary and revocable, so coverage depends on continued lab cooperation.

**Connections:**

- → NAAIMES (ex-AISI Network): UK AISI is a founding network member
- → US Frontier AI Access EO: 30-day access model mirrors UK AISI voluntary access agreements
- → UK AI Bill: AI Bill would put AISI on a statutory footing
- → Anthropic RSP: UK AISI tested Anthropic models pre-deployment
- → OpenAI Preparedness: UK AISI tested OpenAI models pre-deployment
- → GDM Frontier Safety Framework: UK AISI tested DeepMind models pre-deployment
- → UK Ofcom: Complementary UK AI institutions — Ofcom on content, AISI on capabilities
- → UK ICO: Complementary UK AI regulators — ICO on data, AISI on capabilities

---

#### US CAISI

- Jurisdiction: US Federal
- Enforceability: Soft / advisory
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://www.nist.gov/caissi

Renamed from US AISI in Jun 2025. Within NIST. Mission rewritten to drop "safety" framing, but active pre-deployment testing capacity returned in 2026. Relabelled Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI) on NIST's site after EO 14434 (29 Sep 2026) replaced "AI" with "Super Intelligence" in executive-branch usage.

Reframed as the Center for AI Standards and Innovation; standards-setting (model evaluation methodology, benchmarking) initially supplanted direct frontier-model testing. But May 2026 brought a partial reversal: CAISI published a DeepSeek V4 Pro evaluation and announced new pre-deployment testing agreements with Google DeepMind, Microsoft, and xAI. Now operates as a hybrid — selective frontier testing alongside standards work, complementing third-party evaluators (METR, Apollo, AVERI).

**Coverage:**

- *Model evaluations*: Standards work via NIST (model evaluation methodology, benchmarking) plus selective frontier testing — published a DeepSeek V4 Pro evaluation in May 2026 and holds new pre-deployment testing agreements with Google DeepMind, Microsoft, and xAI.
- *Accountability*: Standards-setting via NIST functions as soft accountability — published methodologies are widely adopted but carry no enforcement. Direct evaluation accountability has migrated outside the agency.

**Connections:**

- → NAAIMES (ex-AISI Network): CAISI represents the US in the network
- → US EO 14179: EO led to AISI rename to CAISI in Jun 2025
- → NIST AI RMF: CAISI sits within NIST alongside the AI RMF
- → Frontier Security Institute: Both work on national-security review of frontier models

---

#### Other national AISIs

- Jurisdiction: Multilateral
- Enforceability: Soft / advisory
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://www.gov.uk/government/news/efforts-to-share-best-practices-on-ai-measurement-and-evaluations-driven-forward-through-the-international-network-for-advanced-ai-measurement-evalua

Singapore (DTC + AI Verify), Japan (J-AISI), France (INESIA), Korea, Canada, Australia, Kenya, India (IndiaAISI).

Capacity varies substantially: Singapore's DTC + AI Verify package is the most operational (active testing); France's INESIA (run by DGE and SGDSN with ANSSI, Inria, LNE and PEReN) is building a national evaluation capacity; J-AISI focuses on standards alignment; Indian and African AISIs are still scaling. All but India are members of the AISI Network, which provides distribution; the substantive testing capacity is concentrated in UK/US/Singapore.

**Coverage:**

- *Model evaluations*: National-level frontier model testing varies substantially: Singapore's DTC + AI Verify package is the most operational; J-AISI focuses on standards alignment; INESIA is building national evaluation capacity. India and Africa are still scaling.
- *Capability elicitation*: Various elicitation methodologies in use, often shared through the AISI Network. Capacity concentrated in UK/US/Singapore; other members benefit from network distribution.
- *Timing & frequency*: Pre-deployment access agreements vary by member — Singapore and Japan have working arrangements with regional labs; most other members rely on AISI Network sharing.

**Connections:**

- → NAAIMES (ex-AISI Network): Singapore, Japan, France, Korea, Canada, Australia, Kenya participate
- → Australia eSafety Commissioner: Australia also participates in the AISI Network
- → Singapore IMDA: IMDA hosts Singapore's DTC + AI Verify AISI-equivalent work
- → Japan sectoral AI regulators: J-AISI is Japan's central institute alongside sectoral ministries

---

#### METR

- Jurisdiction: Corporate / global
- Enforceability: Voluntary
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://metr.org/

Independent evaluator. Authors the "Common Elements" analysis itself.

Specialises in autonomous-task evaluation — measuring how long, how reliably, and how independently a model can complete real software-engineering, research, or operational tasks. Maintains the cross-lab catalogue of capability thresholds that the orthogonal view of this map uses. The 'common elements' analysis is the conceptual taxonomy that surfaced the gaps between lab frameworks. May 2026 Frontier Risk Report introduced entity-based assessments — evaluating internal-use risks across Anthropic, Google, Meta, and OpenAI as a new modality alongside model-evaluation work.

**Coverage:**

- *Capability thresholds*: Maintains the cross-lab catalogue of capability thresholds that the orthogonal view of this map uses. The Common Elements analysis identified gaps and inconsistencies between lab frameworks that prompted SB 53 and EU GPAI Code drafting.
- *Model evaluations*: Independent capability evaluations conducted under access agreements with frontier labs (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind). Specialises in autonomous-task evaluation — measuring how long, how reliably, and how independently a model can complete real tasks.
- *Capability elicitation*: Specialises in autonomous-task elicitation — agentic scaffolding, long-horizon task completion, and capability discovery in real software-engineering and research workflows. Distinct from Apollo's scheming-detection focus.

**Connections:**

- → Intl AI Safety Report: METR contributes capability evidence to AISR
- → Anthropic RSP: METR conducts capability evaluations for Anthropic
- → OpenAI Preparedness: METR conducts capability evaluations for OpenAI
- → GDM Frontier Safety Framework: METR conducts capability evaluations for DeepMind
- → AVERI: AVERI builds on METR's evaluation work

---

#### Apollo Research

- Jurisdiction: Corporate / global
- Enforceability: Voluntary
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://www.apolloresearch.ai/

Independent evaluator focused on deceptive alignment. Findings shaped lab eval suites and Intl AI Safety Report.

Researches whether frontier models will scheme — strategically deceive evaluators, exfiltrate, or sandbag during testing. Published the 2024 paper that brought scheming evaluations into mainstream lab practice; findings flagged in the Feb 2026 Intl AI Safety Report sandbagging discussion. Influence is methodological rather than scaled: a small lab whose evaluation approach has been adopted across the field.

**Coverage:**

- *Model evaluations*: Specialised evaluations focused on deceptive alignment, scheming, and sandbagging. Findings flagged in the Feb 2026 Intl AI Safety Report sandbagging discussion.
- *Capability elicitation*: Established the dominant external methodology for scheming detection — controlled stress-tests for whether models strategically deceive evaluators, exfiltrate, or sandbag. The conceptual frame (deceptive alignment, mesa-optimisation) predates Apollo, but their 2024 paper was the inflection point that brought scheming evaluations into mainstream lab practice — cited as input to GDM's FSF v2, used in OpenAI's o1 system card and Preparedness v2, and referenced in Anthropic's Claude system cards.

**Connections:**

- → Intl AI Safety Report: Apollo contributes scheming evidence to AISR
- → Anthropic RSP: Apollo evaluates Anthropic models for scheming
- → GDM Frontier Safety Framework: Apollo evaluates DeepMind models for scheming
- → AVERI: AVERI builds on Apollo's evaluation work

---

#### AVERI

- Jurisdiction: Corporate / global
- Enforceability: Voluntary
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://www.averi.org/

AI Verification and Evaluation Research Institute (Jan 2026, Brundage). Targets the auditing-capacity bottleneck.

501(c)(3) launched Jan 15, 2026 by Miles Brundage (formerly OpenAI policy lead). Published an 'AI Assurance Levels' framework on launch — analogous to safety integrity levels in other industries — designed to give regulators and labs a shared scaffold for third-party auditing. Aimed squarely at the bottleneck the EU AI Act exposes: there are far more obligations to verify than independent auditors qualified to verify them.

**Coverage:**

- *Model evaluations*: Third-party verification capacity for AI assurance — analogous to safety integrity levels in other industries. Aimed at the bottleneck the EU AI Act exposes: more obligations to verify than independent auditors qualified to verify them.
- *Accountability*: Independent verification mechanism for frontier AI assurance. Builds on METR and Apollo evaluation work; develops audit standards and policy requirements, informed by voluntary pilot audits with leading labs (e.g. a 2026 double-blind evaluation of a Gemini model with Google DeepMind).

**Connections:**

- → METR: AVERI builds on METR's evaluation work
- → Apollo Research: AVERI builds on Apollo's evaluation work

---

#### Center for AI Safety

- Jurisdiction: Corporate / global
- Enforceability: Voluntary
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://www.safe.ai/

Independent AI safety nonprofit (501(c)(3)), founded 2022 by Dan Hendrycks. Authored the May 2023 "Statement on AI Risk" signed by hundreds of AI leaders.

Field-building NGO running widely-used safety benchmarks (MMLU, Humanity's Last Exam, WMDP weapons-of-mass-destruction proxy), research grants, and policy advocacy. The May 2023 'Statement on AI Risk' — a one-sentence declaration that mitigating extinction risk from AI should be a global priority — was signed by leading lab CEOs (Altman, Hassabis, Amodei) and shaped the 2023-2024 AI-risk discourse. In June 2026 expanded leadership with former xAI engineer Devin Kim as President and established the Frontier Security Institute as a DC-based national-security affiliate.

**Coverage:**

- *Model evaluations*: Hosts and publishes safety benchmarks (MMLU, Humanity's Last Exam, WMDP) that feed into lab framework evaluations and AISI testing.
- *Capability elicitation*: WMDP and adjacent benchmarks operationalise capability elicitation for biorisk and cyber-misuse scenarios.
- *Accountability*: May 2023 Statement on AI Risk created a high-profile accountability moment; ongoing field-building, policy advocacy, and grant-making across the AI safety ecosystem.
- *Updating policies*: Benchmarks revised as evaluation methodology matures; new ones (HLE, WMDP) added through 2024-2026.

**Connections:**

- → Frontier Security Institute: FSI is CAIS's DC-based national-security affiliate
- → Intl AI Safety Report: CAIS's 2023 Statement on AI Risk shaped the discourse the AISR formalises

---

#### Frontier Security Institute

- Jurisdiction: Corporate / global
- Enforceability: Voluntary
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://frontiersecurityinstitute.org/

CAIS affiliate launched June 2, 2026 in Washington, DC. Translates between frontier AI developers and the US national-security enterprise.

Sits between frontier labs and US national-security institutions — the Pentagon, intelligence community, and Congress. Led by Executive Director Ike Harris (former US Navy / SecDef policy advisor), COO Jeremy Pelter (former Acting Commerce Secretary), and research director Aaron Frank (former RAND). Three named focus areas: securing advanced model weights, how national-security operators test and use frontier models, and AI's effect on geopolitical stability. Unlike general third-party evaluators (METR, Apollo, AVERI), FSI's evaluations are scoped to national-security use cases, alongside policy analysis, wargames and model-security work with the labs.

**Coverage:**

- *Model evaluations*: Offers independent, non-commercial capability assessments scoped to national-security use cases and develops test-and-evaluation criteria for government use of frontier models; standing advisory can include classified-context engagement.
- *Weight security*: Securing advanced AI model weights against state-actor exfiltration is one of FSI's three named focus areas — bridges lab weight-security commitments and US national-security review.
- *Accountability*: Policy translation between frontier labs and US national-security institutions; aims to make lab safety commitments legible to national-security review processes.

**Connections:**

- → Center for AI Safety: FSI is CAIS's DC-based national-security affiliate
- → US CAISI: Both work on national-security review of frontier models
- → US Frontier AI Access EO: FSI's lab–national-security translation bears on the EO's voluntary frontier-model access framework

---

#### UK Ofcom

- Jurisdiction: United Kingdom
- Enforceability: Binding with penalties
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://www.ofcom.org.uk/online-safety

Communications regulator with AI-specific enforcement authority under the Online Safety Act 2023. Fines up to £18M or 10% of global revenue.

Originally telecoms and broadcasting regulator; the Online Safety Act 2023 added enforcement authority over illegal content, including AI-generated harmful content (deepfakes, non-consensual intimate imagery, CSAM, fraud), on regulated user-to-user and search services, with extra duties for Category 1 services. The Illegal Content Codes of Practice (in force Mar 2025) recommend measures such as CSAM hash matching but contain no AI-specific provisions. The Crime and Policing Act 2026 lets the Secretary of State extend the Act's illegal-content duties and Ofcom's enforcement powers to AI services, such as chatbots, by regulations. Shapes how labs ship image/video generators into the UK market, even though it doesn't target frontier developers directly.

**Coverage:**

- *Timing & frequency*: Post-deployment monitoring of online services, with takedown obligations for AI-generated illegal content.
- *Deployment mitigations*: Codes of Practice recommend (rather than mandate) measures such as CSAM hash matching and swift takedown, plus age assurance under the children's codes; an NCII hash-matching measure was added in 2026. Following them counts as compliance. No AI-specific measures such as content authentication.
- *Accountability*: Ofcom can issue fines up to £18M or 10% of global revenue, plus business-disruption orders. Among the most enforceable AI-content regimes in any common-law jurisdiction.

**Connections:**

- → UK AISI: Complementary UK AI institutions — Ofcom on content, AISI on capabilities
- → UK AI Bill: UK AI Bill would clarify the boundary between Ofcom (content) and AISI (frontier)
- → Australia eSafety Commissioner: Parallel online-safety regulators with AI-specific authority

---

#### UK ICO

- Jurisdiction: United Kingdom
- Enforceability: Binding with penalties
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/artificial-intelligence/

Information Commission (took over from the Information Commissioner on 30 Sep 2026; still branded ICO) — data protection regulator applying UK GDPR to AI, with non-statutory AI guidance. Fines up to £17.5M or 4% of global turnover.

Regulates how organisations train on, deploy, and explain AI under UK GDPR. Its Guidance on AI and Data Protection (2020, updated 2023), part of its AI auditing framework, sets out how it interprets the law on lawful basis, fairness, transparency, and Data Protection Impact Assessments for AI systems; it is not a statutory code and is under review after the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. Has investigated Clearview AI, Snap My AI, and others — operates as the UK's de facto frontier-AI privacy regulator alongside any future AISI statutory mandate.

**Coverage:**

- *Model evaluations*: Data Protection Impact Assessments are required for high-risk AI processing; the AI Auditing Framework specifies evaluation methodology.
- *Deployment mitigations*: Non-statutory guidance on fairness, transparency, lawful basis, and explainability for AI deployments touching personal data; the underlying UK GDPR duties are binding.
- *Accountability*: Investigations and fines up to £17.5M or 4% of global revenue; operates as the UK's privacy-rights regulator for AI.

**Connections:**

- → UK AISI: Complementary UK AI regulators — ICO on data, AISI on capabilities
- → UK AI Bill: UK AI Bill would clarify ICO's role alongside AISI
- → EU AI Act: UK GDPR/ICO guidance and EU AI Act set parallel data/AI standards

---

#### US FTC

- Jurisdiction: US Federal
- Enforceability: Hard law, weak enforcement
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/blog/ai-tools-and-related-products-services

Federal Trade Commission enforces consumer-protection law against deceptive or unfair AI practices under Section 5. No AI-specific statutory authority.

Active enforcement against deceptive AI claims and harmful AI deployments under existing consumer-protection authority. Operation AI Comply (Sept 2024) brought five cases against AI hype, fake reviews, and unsubstantiated claims (the current Commission set aside the Rytr order in Dec 2025 as an unnecessary burden on AI innovation); the Rite Aid biometric AI case (2024) banned facial recognition use for five years. Less direct frontier-developer relevance than the EU AI Office, but shapes deployment practice through enforcement signals. Now enlisted in the federal preemption push: EO 14365 directed it to explain when Section 5 preempts state laws requiring altered AI outputs, and its July 2026 proposed policy statement says such laws are impliedly preempted where they require deception.

**Coverage:**

- *Deployment mitigations*: Enforcement against deceptive AI claims, fake reviews, harmful AI deployments, and biometric-AI misuse.
- *Accountability*: Section 5 enforcement; consent decrees with operational restrictions (e.g., the Rite Aid five-year facial-recognition ban).
- *Updating policies*: AI enforcement priorities published in FTC business guidance and AI-specific blog posts.

**Connections:**

- → US AI Action Plan: FTC operates alongside the Action Plan, enforcing federal consumer law on AI
- → US preemption EO: EO 14365 directs the FTC to explain when Section 5 preempts state AI-output laws; FTC proposed that policy statement in Jul 2026

---

#### Australia eSafety Commissioner

- Jurisdiction: Asia-Pacific (other)
- Enforceability: Binding with penalties
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://www.esafety.gov.au/industry/codes

World's first online safety regulator (established 2015), with AI-specific enforcement authority under the Online Safety Act 2021.

Issues binding industry Codes and Standards (including for AI-generated content) under the Online Safety Act 2021. The 2024 Industry Standards mandate proactive safeguards against AI-generated CSAM and pro-terror material from Designated Internet Services. Takedown powers, civil penalties of up to 30,000 penalty units for breaching an industry standard or a direction to comply with a code (500 for most notice breaches), and business-disruption orders. The leading non-EU model for AI-content regulation with binding effect; influences regulatory templates in the Five Eyes and broader Asia-Pacific.

**Coverage:**

- *Timing & frequency*: Proactive obligations to prevent AI-generated illegal content at design and deployment stages, not just reactive takedowns.
- *Deployment mitigations*: Industry Standards mandate safeguards on AI-generated illegal content (CSAM, pro-terror material) for Designated Internet Services.
- *Accountability*: Civil penalties of up to 30,000 penalty units for breaching an industry standard or a code direction (500 for most notice breaches); takedown notices; service-disruption orders.

**Connections:**

- → UK Ofcom: Parallel online-safety regulators with AI-specific authority
- → Other national AISIs: Australia also participates in the AISI Network

---

#### Colorado Division of Insurance

- Jurisdiction: US State
- Enforceability: Binding with penalties
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://doi.colorado.gov/category/ai

First US state-level sectoral AI regulator. Regulation 10-1-1 (effective Nov 14, 2023) governs algorithm and predictive-model use by insurance carriers.

Predates every comprehensive US state AI law. Requires insurance carriers to implement an algorithm and predictive-model governance framework, conduct bias testing, document model assumptions, and submit attestations — applied to life insurers first (Nov 2023), then extended to private passenger auto and health benefit plan insurers (Oct 2025). Followed by similar adoptions in other states via the NAIC Model Bulletin on AI (Dec 2023). The historical anchor that complicates 'first sectoral AI regulator' claims about later state laws like NY RAISE's DFS office.

**Coverage:**

- *Model evaluations*: Algorithm governance framework with mandatory bias testing and documented model assumptions for in-scope insurance lines.
- *Deployment mitigations*: Risk management framework for predictive models used in insurance underwriting, including data-source review and outcome monitoring.
- *Accountability*: Carrier attestations to the Division of Insurance; sectoral oversight under existing insurance regulatory authority.
- *Updating policies*: Periodic guidance updates; framework adopted as template by other state insurance regulators via NAIC Model Bulletin.

**Connections:**

- → Colorado ADMT Act: Same state, different focus — DOI sectoral framework predates the AI Act
- → NY RAISE Act: Colorado DOI precedent informed NY RAISE's DFS office model

---

#### Singapore IMDA

- Jurisdiction: Asia-Pacific (other)
- Enforceability: Hard law, weak enforcement
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://www.imda.gov.sg/about-imda/emerging-technologies-and-research/artificial-intelligence

Info-communications Media Development Authority — Singapore's main AI governance body. Manages AI Verify and the Model AI Governance Framework.

Originally a telecoms and media regulator; now Singapore's primary AI governance body. Published the Model AI Governance Framework (2019, updated for GenAI in 2024) and operates AI Verify, a standardised testing toolkit adopted by major labs and adapted as a regional template. Convenes the AI Verify Foundation as a multistakeholder body. For financial services, MAS ran its own Veritas initiative (2019–2023) and issued Guidelines on AI Risk Management in Oct 2026 (effective Oct 2027). Singapore's approach emphasises voluntary frameworks plus strong testing infrastructure — a template increasingly referenced across ASEAN.

**Coverage:**

- *Model evaluations*: AI Verify provides a standardised public testing toolkit adopted by major labs; results feed into both regulator and developer assessments.
- *Deployment mitigations*: Model AI Governance Framework sets voluntary deployment expectations on transparency, fairness, accountability, and human oversight — applied across sectors via sectoral adaptations.
- *Accountability*: AI Verify Foundation provides multistakeholder accountability; for finance, MAS's Guidelines on AI Risk Management (effective Oct 2027) set supervisory expectations.
- *Updating policies*: Model framework extended to GenAI in 2024 and to agentic AI in Jan 2026 (updated May 2026); AI Verify continually updated as evaluation methodology matures.

**Connections:**

- → Other national AISIs: IMDA hosts Singapore's DTC + AI Verify AISI-equivalent work
- → Hiroshima Process: Singapore endorses Hiroshima Process voluntary norms
- → Japan sectoral AI regulators: Parallel light-touch sector-driven Asia-Pacific AI governance approach

---

#### Japan sectoral AI regulators

- Jurisdiction: Asia-Pacific (other)
- Enforceability: Soft / advisory
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://www.meti.go.jp/shingikai/mono_info_service/ai_shakai_jisso/20260331_report.html

Sectoral AI guidance from Japan's ministry regulators (METI, FSA, MHLW, MIC) under the AI Promotion Act framework. Soft guidance rather than binding rules.

Japan's AI governance operates sector-by-sector: METI (Economy, Trade and Industry) issues the AI Guidelines for Business and developer-facing principles; FSA (Financial Services Agency) handles AI risk management in finance; MHLW (Health, Labour and Welfare) covers AI in healthcare and employment; MIC (Internal Affairs and Communications) governs AI in telecoms and media. Coordinated through the AI Strategic Headquarters under the Cabinet Office. The deliberately soft approach — voluntary guidelines, no compute thresholds, no fines — mirrors the Hiroshima Process Japan championed at the G7.

**Coverage:**

- *Deployment mitigations*: Sectoral guidance varies by ministry but generally focuses on transparency, explainability, human oversight, and risk management in domain-specific contexts.
- *Accountability*: Sectoral oversight via existing ministry powers; no central AI regulator. Coordination through the AI Strategic Headquarters.
- *Updating policies*: METI's AI Guidelines for Business updated periodically; FSA risk management framework revised as the GenAI landscape evolves.

**Connections:**

- → Singapore IMDA: Parallel light-touch sector-driven Asia-Pacific AI governance approach
- → Japan AI Promotion Act: Sectoral implementation under the AI Promotion Act framework
- → Hiroshima Process: Japan's sectoral approach embeds Hiroshima Process principles
- → Other national AISIs: J-AISI is Japan's central institute alongside sectoral ministries

---

#### US BIS export controls

- Jurisdiction: US Federal
- Enforceability: Binding with penalties
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://www.bis.gov/

Bureau of Industry and Security chip export rules (2022, 2023, 2024). The Jan 2025 AI Diffusion Rule (country tiers, model-weight controls) has not been enforced since May 2025; a Jan 2026 rule moved licences for H200-class chips to China to case-by-case review. Most consequential single piece — shapes who can train at the frontier.

Successive rules tightened export-licence requirements for advanced compute (GPUs, fabrication tools, lithography) to China and other concerns; the Dec 2024 update added controls on high-bandwidth memory and chipmaking equipment. The Jan 2025 AI Diffusion Rule added country tiers and a licence requirement for closed model weights trained on more than 10²⁶ operations, but BIS stopped enforcing it in May 2025 and said it would rescind and replace it. May 31, 2026 guidance closed a key loophole by confirming the ultimate-parent-company test applies — any subsidiary worldwide whose ultimate parent is in the restricted countries list needs a US license. Operates outside the safety-regulation framing — its lever is who can build frontier models at all, not what they must do once built. The single most consequential piece of US AI policy by impact, even though it isn't framed as 'AI regulation.'

**Coverage:**

- *Capability thresholds*: Chip-performance thresholds (total processing performance) govern export-licence requirements for advanced GPUs; separate controls cover fabrication tools and lithography. The Jan 2025 AI Diffusion Rule's model-weight threshold (more than 10²⁶ training operations) is not being enforced.
- *Weight security*: Restricts adversaries from training-frontier-capable hardware — adjacent to but distinct from weight security. The lever is who can build frontier models at all, not what they must do once built.

---

#### NIST AI RMF

- Jurisdiction: US Federal
- Enforceability: Soft / advisory
- Status: In force
- Primary source: https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework

NIST AI Risk Management Framework (2023, GenAI Profile 2024); being revised under the White House AI Action Plan, with a Critical Infrastructure Profile in development (concept note Apr 2026). De facto global reference.

Voluntary framework structured around four functions — Govern, Map, Measure, Manage — applied across the AI lifecycle. Embedded into procurement, agency policy, and corporate compliance programs even outside the US. Doesn't impose obligations itself but is referenced by sector regulators (financial, healthcare) and informs the EU GPAI Code structure.

**Coverage:**
